overview:
On 30 January 1933 Adolf Hitler was appointed chancellor of a Germany that was still, on paper, a parliamentary republic. Within six months it was not. A fire in the Reichstag building at the end of February gave the pretext for an emergency decree suspending civil liberties; the Enabling Act of 23 March let the cabinet legislate without parliament; by mid-July the Nazi Party was the only legal party in the country. What followed was called Gleichschaltung, "coordination" — trade unions, state governments, courts, universities, newspapers, sporting clubs and churches were absorbed, purged or intimidated into line. The first concentration camps opened that spring as improvised local prisons for Communists, Social Democrats and other opponents before hardening into a permanent SS system. In June 1934 Hitler had the leadership of his own paramilitary SA murdered along with other inconvenient figures, and when President Hindenburg died that August he fused the presidency with the chancellorship and took the army's personal oath of loyalty.

The regime built its domestic support on recovery and revision. Public works, rearmament and deficit spending pulled Germany out of mass unemployment, and each foreign-policy gamble that the Versailles powers failed to answer — conscription and an announced air force in 1935, the remilitarisation of the Rhineland in 1936, the annexation of Austria and the Sudetenland in 1938, the seizure of the rest of Czechoslovakia in 1939 — made Hitler look infallible. Underneath, exclusion of Jews from German economic, professional and civic life ran continuously from 1933, formalised in the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 and made violent in the November 1938 pogrom. The invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939 began the European war. After early victories in Scandinavia, the Low Countries and France, the attack on the Soviet Union in June 1941 turned the war into the campaign of racial conquest and starvation that Nazi ideology had always envisaged, and it was in the occupied east that mass shootings and then the death camps carried out the murder of roughly six million European Jews, alongside Roma, Soviet prisoners of war, disabled Germans, Poles, political prisoners and others.

Germany lost the initiative in 1943 and was ground down between Soviet armies in the east, Anglo-American forces in the west and bombing from the air. An army-led attempt to kill Hitler in July 1944 failed and was answered with executions. Hitler killed himself in Berlin on 30 April 1945; the surrender took effect on 8 May. The country that emerged was occupied, partitioned among four powers, stripped of its eastern provinces and emptied of some twelve million ethnic Germans expelled westward. The Allies pursued denazification and tried surviving leaders at Nuremberg. Twelve years of rule had killed tens of millions of people across Europe, including several million Germans, and left the state itself extinguished.
significance: Nazi Germany is the reference point against which modern politics measures its worst possibilities: it showed that an industrialised, literate, legally sophisticated European state could dismantle its own constitution through mostly legal steps in a matter of months, and then organise mass murder with bureaucratic and technological method. The response shaped the institutions we still live inside — the Nuremberg trials and the category of crimes against humanity, the Genocide Convention and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the postwar constraints written into West Germany's Basic Law, and the division of Germany and Europe that structured the Cold War for forty years. It also permanently changed how historians and citizens think about complicity, since the regime's crimes required not only fanatics but a very large number of ordinary administrators, soldiers, businessmen and neighbours.
coverage: Written from the Wikipedia and Britannica overview articles and the US Holocaust Memorial Museum's Holocaust Encyclopedia, plus institutional material on forced labour; the dataset itself holds no events for this story, so nothing here is anchored to a mapped place or date. The documentary record is enormous but uneven — the regime destroyed records as it collapsed, key decisions on the Holocaust were deliberately never written down as explicit orders, and figures for deaths in the occupied Soviet Union, for Roma victims and for German civilian deaths remain estimates that serious historians still dispute by millions. Questions of how much ordinary Germans knew and supported are argued over rather than settled.
